title: Encrypted traffic: what can still be seen
quick: Encrypted traffic hides its content, but an investigator can often still see who connected to whom, when, how much data moved, and sometimes the server name used in the handshake.

sections.title: What TLS does
text: TLS is the protocol behind HTTPS and many other secure services. It protects the content of a connection from being read or changed on the way. In TLS 1.3, all handshake messages after the ServerHello are encrypted (RFC 8446).
Without the keys, you cannot read the content, so a capture shows only protected data.

sections.title: What stays visible
text: Even when content is hidden, other details remain. These are called metadata.
points: Source and destination addresses and ports.
Time, duration and amount of data.
DNS lookups made before the connection.
The first message of the handshake, the ClientHello, which is not encrypted and can carry a server name.
Certificate details in older TLS versions.

sections.title: Reading the content
text: Content can be read only if you have the session keys or the private key in a case where that is possible. Some clients can write session keys to a file for testing, and Wireshark can use such a file. Modern key exchange often makes a stolen server key alone not enough.
Other routes are the endpoint itself, such as memory or logs on the device. Procedures and laws differ by country and agency, so follow your lab's own procedure.

sections.title: Practical advice
text: Do not try to break encryption in routine cases. Use the metadata, the endpoint evidence and other logs together. Document what you could and could not see.

mistakes: Thinking that encrypted means nothing can be learned.
Believing the server name is always hidden.
Expecting to decrypt a capture without session keys.
Forgetting to look at the endpoint, which may hold the keys or the data.

terms.meaning: A protocol that encrypts data between a client and a server.
The first exchange where keys are agreed.
Details about traffic, such as time and size, not the content.
A field in the handshake that names the server the client wants.
A temporary key used to encrypt one connection.

exam.q: What can you learn from encrypted traffic?
exam.a: Addresses, ports, time, volume, DNS lookups and often the server name from the handshake.
The endpoint holds the data before encryption and may hold keys, so its evidence can show what network capture cannot.

sources_note: Written in our own words from public forensic training material and standards.
